findings.detail: November 2025 Audit Wales review identified that the Council has limited recognition and understanding of the Planning Service's role in supporting priorities. The service lacks a service plan, has weak resource management, and limited performance oversight. Four recommendations were made covering resource planning, risk management, performance management, and monitoring of service activity.
findings.matters: A strategic council service operating without a service plan and with weak oversight is a governance gap. Planning drives economic development and can impact council income; weakness here could affect financial performance.
findings.figures: 4 audit recommendations made; service operating without service plan
findings.quote: The review found that the Council has limited recognition and understanding of the important role the service has in supporting its priorities. There are weaknesses in the management of resources and risk to support the service. The service lacks a service plan and there is limited understanding and oversight of the service's performance.

findings.headline: Audit Wales found council lacks arrangements to assure value for money in commissioning services
findings.detail: June 2025 Audit Wales review identified that the Council does not have corporate arrangements to assure it consistently secures value for money when commissioning. Specific gaps include: no process to decide if/how to commission; no requirement for service rationale or intended outcomes; no comprehensive options appraisal; does not understand full costs; and does not consistently consider wider impacts of commissioning decisions.
findings.matters: Absence of value-for-money assurance in commissioning is a material control weakness that could indicate inefficient or wasteful spending across commissioned services.
findings.figures: Multiple commissioning services reviewed; gaps identified across options appraisal, cost understanding, and impact assessment
findings.quote: Overall, the audit found that the Council did not have arrangements to assure itself that it consistently secures value for money when it commissions services.

findings.headline: Internal Audit rated Risk Management as only Limited Assurance
findings.detail: Risk Management is the only audit opinion that received Limited Assurance (2 out of 42 audits; 95% positive overall). The council acknowledges that its risk management culture and systems are underdeveloped and limit its ability to identify, assess and respond to risks affecting strategic objectives. This is being addressed as a priority action for 2026-27.
findings.matters: Limited assurance on risk management is a governance red flag. It suggests the council may not be identifying emerging threats or changes in its operating environment until they become operational problems.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion (1 of 42 audits); 95% of audit opinions were positive overall
findings.quote: Internal Audit's overall opinion of Risk Management was Limited Assurance.

findings.headline: School budgets showing increasing fragility, with schools using reserves to fund activity and risk of going into deficit
findings.detail: Schools are drawing down balances to cover current spending. Schools with projected deficits over 5% of delegated funding have been required to submit recovery plans. This was flagged as a significant issue in 2024-25 and remains ongoing through 2025-26. If schools exhaust reserves, the council may face pressure to provide funding.
findings.matters: School deficits reduce a council's local tax base resilience and may force general fund support. Mass school deficits can indicate systemic problems in education funding or council support levels.
findings.figures: Schools with projected deficits of more than 5% of delegated funding required to submit deficit recovery plans
findings.quote: There is an increase in the financial fragility of schools in the Borough and schools having to use their balances to fund activity with an increased risk of schools going into deficit.

findings.headline: Council must deliver £40 million in savings over four years, 2026-27 to 2029-30
findings.detail: The council faces a significant multi-year savings requirement across the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period. Welsh Government has given no indication of funding levels for future years, forcing the council to work with uncertain assumptions. The council has developed detailed budgets only for 2026-27.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council has a credible plan to deliver material savings over a medium-term horizon without compromising service quality or forcing unsustainable reserves depletion.
findings.figures: £40 million over 2026-27 to 2029-30
findings.quote: The Council estimates that it will need to generate approximately £40 million of savings over the period 2026-27 to 2029-30.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - 2025-26 MTFS Budget Reductions Risk Tracker March 2026
findings.headline: Contingency reserve depleted, leaving reduced financial headroom
findings.detail: The council used £1.543 million from uncommitted MTFS contingency funding (originally £1.63m set aside) to cover emerging pressures in 2025-26. The document explicitly notes 'there is less headroom corporately to deal with unexpected financial pressures going forward,' meaning the council's buffer for shocks has been materially reduced.
findings.matters: Contingency depletion reduces the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or deliver additional savings if required. With a £3.6m school deficit already present, financial headroom is critical.
findings.figures: £1.543 million of contingency used in 2025-26; original MTFS 2024-28 allocation was £1.63m
findings.quote: It does mean, however, that there is less headroom corporately to deal with unexpected financial pressures going forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - 2025-26 MTFS Budget Reductions Risk Tracker March 2026
findings.headline: Safeguarding capacity cuts cancelled after regulatory pushback
findings.detail: The council proposed removing dedicated corporate safeguarding capacity (£57k saving, £0 achieved). The document states this was cancelled because 'recent reviews across Wales have demonstrated the need to strengthen corporate safeguarding responsibilities rather than reducing them.' This indicates regulator concern that the council was cutting essential governance functions.
findings.matters: Regulators intervening to block cuts to safeguarding signals governance weakness. If Wales-wide reviews found councils were cutting safeguarding inadequately, this council's earlier decision to do so raises questions about its own governance practices.
findings.figures: £57k proposed saving not achieved; Welsh Government reviews triggered policy reversal
findings.quote: recent reviews across Wales have demonstrated the need to strengthen corporate safeguarding responsibilities rather than reducing them.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - 2025-26 MTFS Budget Reductions Risk Tracker March 2026
findings.headline: Health and Safety staffing cuts risk HSE prosecution despite recent interventions
findings.detail: The council attempted to cut £76k from the Corporate Health and Safety Unit but only achieved £19k. The document explicitly warns of 'potential serious failings under current health and safety legislation, potentially leading to prosecution (corporate and personal liability for senior officers)' and notes 'there have been several HSE interventions within the last two years.' Despite this, the council is still pursuing reductions.
findings.matters: Active HSE interventions combined with further staffing cuts create material liability risk to the council and personal liability to senior officers. Fines and enforcement action could be unbudgeted.
findings.figures: £76k reduction target, £19k achieved; several HSE interventions noted in last two years
findings.quote: Potential serious failings under the current health and safety legislation, potentially leading to prosecution (corporate and personal liability for senior officers, in particular Corporate Management Board)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - 2025-26 MTFS Budget Reductions Risk Tracker March 2026
findings.headline: Planned budget reductions fell short by £1.134 million in a single year
findings.detail: Bridgend proposed £8,379k of reductions but achieved only £7,245k. The shortfall was covered through one-off vacancies and contingency reserves rather than structural savings. Multiple material proposals were not delivered, including supported living closure (£190k), home remodelling (£198k), and safeguarding capacity review (£57k).
findings.matters: Budget gaps met through temporary vacancies are unsustainable. When posts are eventually filled or turnover normalises, the underlying deficit resurfaces. This exposes a recurring budget risk.
findings.figures: £8,379k target, £7,245k achieved, £1,134k shortfall (13.5%)
findings.quote: GRAND TOTAL REDUCTIONS 8,379 7,245 REDUCTION SHORTFALL 1,134

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - 2025-26 MTFS Budget Reductions Risk Tracker March 2026
findings.headline: Schools sector carrying £3.615 million cumulative deficit
findings.detail: The 1% efficiency cut to school delegated budgets was achieved in cash (£1,186k), but resulted in an overall deficit balance across all schools. This is structural, not one-year, with the document stating 'close monitoring of school budgets will continue going into 2026-27' and flagging ongoing concerns about school sustainability.
findings.matters: A £3.6m deficit in schools indicates the council cannot deliver the required cuts without service deterioration or further unexpected costs. Schools cannot carry structural deficits indefinitely.
findings.figures: £3.615 million overall schools sector deficit; £1.186 million savings achieved from delegated budget cuts
findings.quote: Reduced budgets have resulted in an overall deficit balance for schools at year end of £3.615 million.

findings.headline: Council Fund balance at 2.68% of net budget, below the MTFS minimum target of 5%, and well below prudent levels
findings.detail: The Council Fund balance increased to £10.286 million, representing 2.68% of the net revenue budget for 2025-26 (or 4.0% excluding schools). The council's own MTFS Principle 9 requires 5% minimum. The council notes: 'As budgets incrementally increase annually, it is challenging to keep the Council Fund balance in line with' the 5% target. This is a structural shortfall, not a temporary position.
findings.matters: The council has inadequate liquid reserves to handle unexpected events or service pressures. At 2.68%, it is at risk if there is any adverse movement in the budget.
findings.figures: Council Fund £10.286 million; 2.68% of net budget; 4.0% excluding schools; target is 5%
findings.quote: The Council Fund balance has been increased by £278,000 and now represents 2.68% of the net revenue budget for 2025-26, or 4.0% of the net revenue budget excluding schools. As budgets incrementally increase annually, it is challenging to keep the Council Fund balance in line with MTFS Principle 9 which states that: The Council Fund balance should be set at a prudent but not excessive level. This will normally be maintained at a level of 5% of the Council's net budget, excluding schools.

findings.headline: 2025-26 outturn relies on £13+ million of grant funding maximised in final quarter, including one-off £3.922 million packaging scheme
findings.detail: The improved outturn at year-end was materially dependent on grants maximised in quarter 4, totalling over £13 million. The single largest item is £3.922 million from the UK Packaging Extended Producer Responsibility scheme. The council explicitly states: 'some of the recurrent pressures may need reviewing in future years if the pEPR funding reduces significantly.' Other major grants (Children and Communities, Housing Support, Pathways of Care, education grants) were only confirmed late.
findings.matters: The council's strong outturn is not structural but grant-dependent. If pEPR funding reduces or grants are not repeated, the position will deteriorate. This creates year-on-year uncertainty.
findings.figures: £3.922 million pEPR funding (one-off); £846,000 Children and Communities Grant; £726,000 Pathways of Care Grant; £539,000 Housing Support Grant; £2.395 million late education grants
findings.quote: Introduction of a UK Packaging Extended Producer Responsibility (pEPR) scheme relating to Waste Disposal costs (£3.922 million)... However, it is worth noting that some of the recurrent pressures may need reviewing in future years if the pEPR funding reduces significantly.

findings.headline: 2025-26 budget reduction target of £8.379 million achieved only £7.245 million, missing by £1.134 million (13.5%)
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £8.379 million for 2025-26 and achieved £7.245 million, creating a shortfall of £1.134 million. Additionally, £889,000 of prior-year savings targets remain unmet. Major unachieved savings include a £190,000 proposal the service says is 'no longer deliverable', a £198,000 restructure still pending, and a £109,000 restructure only now implemented.
findings.matters: The council is persistently missing its savings targets. One major proposal is no longer deliverable. This suggests over-optimistic planning or operational constraints preventing delivery.
findings.figures: £1.134 million shortfall in 2025-26 savings (13.5% miss); £889,000 prior-year shortfalls; £190,000 (SSW8 no longer deliverable); £198,000 (SSW7 pending); £109,000 (EEYYP5)
findings.quote: The budget approved for 2025-26 included budget reduction proposals totalling £8.379 million, which is broken down in Appendix 2 and summarised in Table 3 below. The year end position is that £7.245 million has been achieved, leading to an overall shortfall on the savings target of £1.134 million, or 13.53% of the overall reduction target.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements overspending £524,000 as insufficient foster carer capacity forces expensive placements
findings.detail: Care Experienced Children services overspent by £524,000. Independent residential care overspent by £603,000 with 27 children in independent residential care. The council states there is insufficient in-house foster carer capacity and insufficient capacity in independent fostering agencies, forcing children into more expensive residential placements than necessary. Supported living also overspent by £282,000 with 28 placements.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary cost but structural: the council lacks capacity and is paying more for worse outcomes. Children are in residential care instead of foster care because alternatives don't exist.
findings.figures: £524,000 overspend on Care Experienced Children; £603,000 overspend on Independent Residential Care; 27 children in independent residential care; £282,000 Supported Living overspend
findings.quote: There is insufficient capacity in-house and in IFAs which means that some children's needs are being met in a higher, more expensive, tier of service.

findings.headline: Schools collectively ran £3.615 million deficit at year-end after council cut Individual School Budget to achieve savings target
findings.detail: School balances deteriorated by £2.996 million during 2025-26. 36 of 59 schools are in deficit (30 primary, 6 secondary). The council met its £1.186 million efficiency saving target by reducing the Individual School Budget, forcing schools to absorb the reduction. The outturn was only improved to this position by £2.395 million of late Welsh Government grant funding in quarter 4.
findings.matters: Schools cannot run sustainably in deficit. The council has pushed the problem into schools rather than absorbing it centrally. If grant funding is not repeated, schools will struggle to deliver.
findings.figures: £3.615 million school deficit at year-end (opened at £619,000 deficit); £2.996 million deterioration; 36 schools in deficit; £2.395 million grant injection in Q4
findings.quote: Whilst the saving is referenced as having been achieved due to the overall reduction in the Individual Schools Budget (ISB), as referenced in paragraph 3.3.1, the reduced budgets have resulted in an overall deficit balance for schools of £3.615 million.

findings.headline: Additional learning needs services overspending by £823,000 with demand growing 18% in a year, despite grant dependency
findings.detail: Inclusion Group budget overspent by £823,000. Pupil numbers in ALN support increased from 303 (spring 2025) to 357 (spring 2026). The service received £1.157 million in grant funding which prevented an overspend of £1.980 million. But Welsh Government ALN grant reduces to £1.100 million in 2026-27. MTFS includes £1.05 million additional budget pressure for ALN in coming years.
findings.matters: This is a persistent demand-driven overspend now dependent on grant funding that is reducing. A lender needs to understand whether the council can absorb this as grants shrink.
findings.figures: £823,000 overspend; £1.157 million grant funding; pupil numbers 303→357; grant reducing to £1.100 million in 2026-27
findings.quote: The demand is high in particular for pupils requiring neurodevelopmental, behavioural, communication and complex medical support. The number of pupils supported during the spring term 2025 was 303, increasing to 345 during the summer term, 348 during the autumn term, and 357 in Spring 2026.

findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion on risk management is Limited Assurance, below the Reasonable Assurance given for governance
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's overall opinion for the risk management framework is 'Limited Assurance', which is explicitly lower than the 'Reasonable Assurance' rating for governance and controls. This indicates the council has material weaknesses in identifying and managing risks.
findings.matters: A limited assurance rating on risk management signals audit-identified control gaps that could affect the council's financial position or operational resilience; lenders and finance directors rely on audit opinions to identify emerging vulnerabilities.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance (risk management) vs Reasonable Assurance (governance)
findings.quote: Based on the work undertaken by Internal and External Audit the overall opinion for risk management is one of 'Limited Assurance'.

findings.headline: 2026-27 budget is balanced only through £2.348m spending cuts and 4.7% council tax rise, with future funding projections unknown
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that balancing the 2026-27 budget depends on achieving £2.348 million in budget reductions and a 4.7% council tax increase. The council further notes that projections of funding for future years remain unknown and characterises the situation as 'extremely challenging', requiring 'early and strong financial planning'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's ability to balance budgets amid uncertain future government funding; reliance on service cuts and council tax rises suggests limited headroom if funding constraints worsen.
findings.figures: £2.348 million budget reductions required; 4.7% council tax increase; 2026-27 budget
findings.quote: Going forward the situation remains challenging with the budget for 2026-27 balanced on the basis of achieving £2.348 million of budget reductions and a council tax increase of 4.7%. Projections of funding for future years are still unknown but the situation looks extremely challenging and early and strong financial planning will be essential to setting a balanced budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - BCBC Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Corporate Risk Management lacks designated accountability and is not being monitored at senior management level
findings.detail: Audit identified multiple structural failures: no single officer with sole responsibility for corporate risks, senior officers who should support risk owners were not identified, risk management software implementation requires prioritization, and there is no documented evidence that corporate risks are being reported and monitored at Senior Management Team, Directorate, Cabinet, or Overview and Scrutiny level. Corporate risks are also not correctly identifiable within Directorate Business Plans.
findings.matters: Effective risk management is fundamental to council governance and financial stewardship. Without clear accountability and senior-level monitoring of corporate risks, the council cannot demonstrate it is identifying and managing threats to its objectives and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 1 of 42 audits (2.4%) received Limited Assurance rating for this issue
findings.quote: The absence of a designated officer with sole responsibility for Corporate Risks undermines clear accountability and inconsistent risk management across the Authority.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - BCBC Annual Internal Audit Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Awen Cultural Trust savings agreed in February 2024 were not identified or achieved
findings.detail: Internal audit found that planned savings included in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy were not realised. The council is also not receiving key governance information from Awen, no updates on partnership performance have been provided to Scrutiny or Cabinet, and the Advisory Board membership and Terms of Reference are outdated.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a council can deliver planned savings and maintain effective oversight of arm's-length bodies. Unachieved savings targets and poor governance of cultural partnerships indicate execution risk and weak control.
findings.figures: Savings agreed February 2024, no value stated in document
findings.quote: The savings in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy, agreed by Council in February 2024, had not been identified or achieved.

findings.headline: High maintenance backlog and aging infrastructure infrastructure create ongoing cost pressure
findings.detail: Much of the highways infrastructure in the northern half of the County Borough dates from the early 1900s and was not designed for current demands. The Council acknowledges a "currently known high level of maintenance backlog." Infrastructure is continuously growing with no sign of abatement. Health and safety works are prioritised in a formal matrix, but other maintenance is deferred.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance represents a future cost liability that could materialise as emergency spending, and aging infrastructure increases operational risk for service delivery.
findings.figures: No backlog value quantified, but flagged as 'high'
findings.quote: Much of the infrastructure serving the northern half of the county borough was originally constructed in the early 1900's and was not designed to cope with the current demands (economic, social and environmental) placed upon it. Given the limited capital and revenue funding and the currently known high level of maintenance backlog, a prioritisation matrix for budget allocation has been developed.

findings.headline: Diminishing reserves and limited asset disposal options constrain financial flexibility
findings.detail: Capital receipts from asset disposals are declining (closing balance forecast to fall from £32.02m in 2025-26 to £4.77m by 2029-30). Uncommitted earmarked reserves are diminishing. The Council has limited capital assets it can sell. This leaves the Council with few internal resources to meet unexpected pressures or take advantage of opportunities.
findings.matters: Limited reserves mean the Council is increasingly dependent on borrowing and grants, and has little buffer to absorb cost overruns, delivery delays, or unexpected demands.
findings.figures: Capital receipts: £21.38m (2025-26) down to £4.77m (2029-30); investment portfolio value £4.89m
findings.quote: Given the uncertainty over future capital receipts, diminishing uncommitted earmarked reserves and limited capital budget allocations from Welsh Government, this will mean that there is limited scope for new capital projects unless fully funded from grants and external contributions.

findings.headline: Tender price inflation is causing capital schemes to exceed available budgets
findings.detail: The Council is receiving tender prices higher than expected for construction works and materials. Supply chain difficulties, material price increases, inability to recruit skilled workers, and additional net zero requirements are all driving costs above forecasts. The document warns that schemes may need to be reprioritised if procurement reveals costs in excess of available budget.
findings.matters: This creates delivery risk: major capital programmes like the schools modernisation could experience cost overruns or slippage, potentially requiring additional borrowing or deferral of planned work.
findings.figures: No specific overrun figures given, but £121.82m capital programme is at risk from cost inflation
findings.quote: Within the current climate tender prices are being received that are higher than expected, with costs potentially exceeding available budgets. Given the uncertainty over future capital receipts, diminishing uncommitted earmarked reserves and limited capital budget allocations from Welsh Government, this will mean that there is limited scope for new capital projects unless fully funded from grants and external contributions.

findings.headline: £16.2 million new borrowing for school modernisation programme
findings.detail: Sustainable Communities for Learning Band B will cost £106.62 million across 2026-27 to 2027-28, plus £3.30 million for associated highways. This is the core of a £121.82 million capital programme. The Council will need to borrow £16.2 million to fund the new school projects. Capital Financing Requirement will increase by £16.31 million in 2026-27 alone.
findings.matters: This is a material, multi-year debt commitment that will lock in revenue obligations for servicing these loans across the forecast period.
findings.figures: £106.62 million schools; £3.30 million highways; £16.20 million new borrowing; CFR increase £16.31 million in 2026-27
findings.quote: The Council will need to borrow approximately £16.20 million in order to fund new school projects in line with the Council's Schools Modernisation Programme.

findings.headline: Welsh Government's Net Zero mandate will drive unfunded capital cost increases across council assets
findings.detail: The strategy notes that Welsh Government's net zero commitment for the public sector will require changes to how assets are designed and managed, explicitly stating this will result in increased capital costs. The strategy does not indicate corresponding funding growth to offset this.
findings.matters: Mandated cost increases that must be absorbed from a funding envelope that is only growing modestly (£0.22m) creates a real affordability risk for the capital programme.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: Additional requirements on schemes to achieve Welsh Government's Net Zero commitment, which includes an aim of collectively achieving net zero across the Welsh public sector, which will likely result in increased costs.

findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk identified if council fails to balance budget or manage increased financial pressures
findings.detail: The risk register states that if the council fails to balance its budget or manage increased financial and service pressures, the Section 151 Officer would have to issue a Sec 114 notice. This would result in government-appointed commissioners taking over management of the council.
findings.matters: A Sec 114 notice is the statutory marker of a council in financial crisis; this is a forward-looking warning that the council recognises this as a material risk if current mitigation fails.
findings.figures: Sec 114 notice threshold identified
findings.quote: Ultimately if the Council fails to balance its budget or manage the increased pressures, the Sec 151 Officer would have to issue a Sec114 notice which could result in the management of the council being undertaken by Commissioners appointed by the government.

findings.headline: Health and social care capacity remains at maximum risk (25) despite action plans affecting hospital discharge
findings.detail: Insufficient community health and social care capacity prevents hospital discharge and community-based support. Despite implementing enhancement actions (additional care home capacity, discharge-to-recover pathways), the residual risk remains at maximum (25, unchanged from previous), indicating actions are not sufficient to resolve the underlying problem.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand demand pressures the council cannot control; persistent high-risk service capacity issues can affect council spending, reputational risk, and potential intervention from Welsh Government.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 25 (unchanged); affects hospital discharge and community capacity
findings.quote: The system has experienced significant pressures so despite the actions the residual risk remains at a very high level and the service continues to evaluate whether immediate actions have impacted.

findings.headline: Capital investment will be constrained due to reduced capital finance, increased borrowing costs, and construction inflation
findings.detail: The council faces reduced external grants, increased borrowing costs, and significantly higher construction and tender prices. Projects are experiencing cost overruns, contractors are harder to find, and the capital earmarked reserve may not be fully replenished due to revenue budget pressures. Infrastructure deterioration poses safety and financial risks.
findings.matters: A lender assesses capital adequacy and investment capacity; reduced capital spending affects the council's ability to maintain critical infrastructure (roads, streetlights, school buildings, technology) and increases deferred maintenance risk.
findings.figures: Costs of projects have risen significantly; capital earmarked reserve may be challenging to replenish due to revenue pressures
findings.quote: Due to reduced capital finance, the Council will have to prioritise more effectively and there is a risk of reduced investment in important infrastructure moving forward.

findings.headline: School financial fragility is increasing, with deficits increasingly difficult to address as funding reduces
findings.detail: Schools are using reserves to fund activity, creating an increased risk of deficits. Schools must resolve deficits within 3 years (or 5 in exceptional cases). The council is undertaking work to review the impact of budget reductions on individual schools and school deficits, indicating a worsening problem.
findings.matters: School deficits become a potential call on the council's resources and complicate overall budget balance; the risk score (25, highest level) is unchanged, meaning the situation is not improving despite mitigation efforts.
findings.figures: Schools must address deficits within 3 years, 5 in exceptional circumstances; residual risk score 25 (unchanged)
findings.quote: Whilst the council seeks to mitigate the impact of the overall financial positions for schools, financial planning has included the need to reduce the level of financial support previously given to schools. The consequences of this include schools having to use their balances to fund activity with increased risk of schools going into deficit.

findings.headline: Welsh Government funding becomes challenging for 2027-28 onwards, following an improved 2026-27 settlement
findings.detail: The council received a better-than-expected 2026-27 settlement, but faces challenging longer-term funding predictions from Welsh Government for 2027-28 onwards due to wider public sector funding shortages. This creates a forward-looking fiscal cliff after the current planning period.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's funding sustainability beyond the current medium-term financial strategy period; funding uncertainty after 2027-28 directly threatens the council's ability to maintain a balanced budget.
findings.figures: Better than expected settlement for 2026-27; longer term predictions challenging for 2027-28 onwards
findings.quote: due to funding shortages across the public sector, the longer term predictions with regards to funding to be received from Welsh Government are challenging for 2027-28 onwards

findings.headline: Capital receipts from asset sales are declining, making the £46m capital programme reserve critical
findings.detail: The council's capital programme reserve now holds £46.083m (69% of all earmarked reserves) and is increasingly important because 'the potential to generate capital receipts from the sale of assets diminishes'. This single reserve is now the main funding source for capital schemes, replacing asset sales as the historic source.
findings.matters: A council whose capital funding is dependent on a single time-limited reserve rather than ongoing income is at risk of having to choose between borrowing (increasing revenue costs) or cancelling capital schemes
findings.figures: Capital programme reserve: £46.083m (69% of £66.783m total earmarked reserves as at 31 December 2025). Remaining earmarked reserves for other commitments: ~£21m.
findings.quote: As the potential to generate capital receipts from the sale of assets diminishes, this has become an important source of funding for the capital programme and enables major capital schemes to progress without the need for borrowing which would put additional pressure on the revenue budget.

findings.headline: Future school budgets face efficiency savings from 2028-29 onwards, despite current freeze
findings.detail: While schools are being protected from budget reductions in 2026-27 and 2027-28, the council explicitly warns that schools must plan for efficiency savings from 2028-29 onwards. The current protection is temporary and contingent on the broader budget position not deteriorating further.
findings.matters: Schools education spending (£126.3m, 33% of net budget) is the largest single budget line; future cuts to schools signal the council's budget headroom has run out and core services will need to shrink
findings.figures: School net budget: £126.309m of £383.226m total net budget (33%). School delegated budget 2026-27: £130m. Additional funding for schools 2026-27: ~£8m net, including ~£5m for pay and price increases.
findings.quote: The forecast pressure on Council budgets for future years is such that further efficiency savings may be unavoidable for schools from 2028-29 onwards, and so it will be necessary for headteachers and governing bodies to plan ahead.

findings.headline: The £42m Band B schools modernisation programme faces significant cost pressures from inflation
findings.detail: The Sustainable Communities for Learning Band B programme, with a provisional commitment of £42m (£15m more than previously committed), is experiencing significant cost pressures due to high inflation affecting tender prices. Full business cases are pending submission to Welsh Government, which means costs could shift further.
findings.matters: A large capital programme with open-ended inflation exposure and funding not yet confirmed represents a material contingent liability; overruns would either require additional borrowing or reductions in the revenue budget
findings.figures: Band B commitment: £42m (£15m increase from prior year). Band A already spent: £21.6m. Programme spans several years with substantial Welsh Government match funding.
findings.quote: We are aware that there are significant cost pressures on this programme due to the impact of high inflation on tender prices being submitted and how this is affecting current costings for this programme.

findings.headline: Council tax collection rate is declining due to residents' economic difficulties
findings.detail: The council reports a reduction in council tax collection rate driven by the cost-of-living crisis, with residents finding it harder to pay. This is coupled with anticipated increases in council tax support, as more residents claim benefits or fall into low-income brackets.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates on a revenue source that is already 28% of the budget creates a compounding pressure: residents have less capacity to pay, the council's income falls, and demand for council tax support simultaneously rises
findings.figures: No specific collection rate percentage provided. Described as 'reduction' due to 'difficult economic circumstances'.
findings.quote: More recently, a reduction in the council tax collection rate, due to the difficult economic circumstances that people find themselves in. This is coupled with a potential increase in council tax support as more people find themselves on low incomes or claiming benefits during the cost of living crisis.

findings.headline: Welsh Government funding is falling in real terms, forcing greater reliance on council tax
findings.detail: Real-terms decline in Welsh Government funding has forced the council to increase the proportion of the net revenue budget funded by council tax, from 25.29% in 2015-16 to 27.84% in 2025-26—a shift of 2.55 percentage points. Council tax is now funding 28p of every pound spent, up from 23p a decade ago. The council tax collection rate has also declined due to residents' economic difficulties.
findings.matters: Deteriorating real funding from Welsh Government combined with declining collection rates and the political limits to council tax increases mean the council's fiscal options are narrowing; service cuts or borrowing may become necessary
findings.figures: WG funding 2015-16: £188.409m; 2025-26: £276.528m (nominal +46.77%, but real decline). Council tax as % of net budget: 25.29% (2015-16) to 27.84% (2025-26). Council tax per Band D: £1,297.78 (2016-17) to £1,916.96 (2025-26). 10-year increase: 4.4% average annual rise.
findings.quote: In real terms, Welsh Government (WG) funding is falling year on year and this has impacted on the proportion of funding that is required to be met from council tax, compared to external WG funding.

findings.headline: Legislative changes in social care are not fully funded by Welsh Government, with transitional funding due to end in 2027-28
findings.detail: The Health and Social Care (Wales) Act 2025 and related legislative changes (removal of profit margins, Real Living Wage requirements) are creating revenue and capital cost pressures that are not fully met by Welsh Government funding. Transitional grant funding to support these changes is scheduled to end in 2027-28, which will increase cost pressures further.
findings.matters: A cliff-edge ending to transitional funding, combined with unfunded mandates, means the council's structural budget deficit will worsen materially in 2027-28 unless offset by savings or service reductions
findings.figures: Transitional funding ends 2027-28. No specific quantum of unfunded cost stated.
findings.quote: Legislative changes are not fully funded by Welsh Government and the removal of profit particularly has significant revenue and capital implications. Grant funding which has been made to support the transitional phase is due to end in 2027-28 which will increase cost pressures.

findings.headline: High-cost children's residential placements continue to exceed budget, including unregistered care settings
findings.detail: The council faces persistent cost pressures from a consistent number of high-cost independent residential placements for children and young people, some in settings that are not registered with Care Inspectorate Wales. These placements continue to exceed budget allocations, and the council is relying on an invest-to-save initiative to reduce reliance on them, indicating current interventions are not working.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled placement costs in children's services are difficult to forecast and represent a liability that can grow rapidly if underlying drivers (numbers of looked-after children, complexity of need, in-house capacity) continue worsening
findings.figures: Not specified in figures; described as 'consistent', 'continuing to exceed budget', with reduction in in-house foster carers exacerbating the need.
findings.quote: There has been a consistent number of high-cost independent residential placements and on occasion 'operating without registration' placements for children and young people. To meet this need the budgetary position has worsened as the number of high cost placements continues to exceed budget.

findings.headline: Council overspent for the first time in its history in 2023-24, requiring wholesale unwinding of earmarked reserves
findings.detail: Bridgend reported an £8.56m overspend in 2023-24—its first ever year-end deficit—and was forced to unwind earmarked reserves to balance the budget. Earmarked reserves fell from £106.73m (2021-22) to £63.99m (2023-24) as a result. This was driven by demand pressures across social services and homelessness that were not budgeted for.
findings.matters: A council with no track record of overspends suddenly requiring emergency reserve drawdowns signals that budget forecasting is breaking down against real demand pressures that were not anticipated
findings.figures: 2023-24 overspend: £8.56m. Earmarked reserves 2023-24: £63.99m (down from £106.73m in 2021-22). Historical position: 2022-23 underspend £1.28m, 2023-24 overspend £8.56m, 2024-25 underspend £12.73m.
findings.quote: In 2023-24 due to the level of demand facing the Council it ended the financial year in an over spend position, the first time in its history. This required the Council to review all of its earmarked reserves and unwind a number of them, in order to balance the budget.

findings.headline: Council Fund balance has fallen below the prudent minimum and continues declining
findings.detail: The Council Fund balance is now 2.6% of net revenue budget (3.9% excluding schools), compared to the stated prudent minimum of 5% in MTFS Principle 9. The document explicitly warns that further drawdowns will put the council's financial sustainability at risk. This represents a four-year decline from £10.11m (2021-22) to £10.01m (2024-25) despite budget growth.
findings.matters: A council drawing down reserves below prudent levels signals declining financial resilience and reduces capacity to absorb unforeseen pressures or service demand spikes
findings.figures: Council Fund balance: 2.6% of net revenue budget, 3.9% excluding schools. Target: 5% of net budget excluding schools. Historical position: £10.11m (2021-22) to £10.01m (2024-25).
findings.quote: Should we continue drawing down from this reserve going forward it will put the financial sustainability of the Council at risk.

findings.headline: LOBO loans (£19.25m) carry refinancing risk if lenders exercise their call options.
findings.detail: The council holds £19.25m in Lender's Option Borrower's Option loans at 4.65% with maturity dates shown as 2054 but subject to rescheduling. The strategy notes that 'With interest rates falling there is a reducing chance that lenders will exercise their options, however this does not preclude them doing so and therefore an element of refinancing risk remains.'
findings.matters: LOBO loans create contingent refinancing risk. If lenders call these loans during a period of rising rates, the council would need to refinance at higher cost or redeploy reserves unexpectedly.
findings.figures: LOBO loans: £19.25m at 4.65% interest, two trigger points annually (July and January)
findings.quote: The LOBO rate and term may vary in the future depending upon the prevailing market rates, the lender exercising their option to increase rates at one of the bi-annual trigger points and therefore the Council being given the option to accept the increase or to repay the loan without incurring a penalty.

findings.headline: Acknowledged significant uncertainty in borrowing forecasts due to volatility in reserves and working capital.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states: 'There is a lot of uncertainly [sic] around the requirement for new borrowing, mainly due to the volatility surrounding financial reserves and working capital.' This undermines confidence in the projection figures themselves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how stable the council's financial position is and whether forecasts can be relied upon. Stated volatility and uncertainty suggest the borrowing figures are directionally correct but not firm commitments.
findings.figures: Not quantified; a statement of forecast uncertainty
findings.quote: There is a lot of uncertainly around the requirement for new borrowing, mainly due to the volatility surrounding financial reserves and working capital.

findings.headline: Multiple capital schemes remain in development stages with expenditure potentially slipping; cost inflation forecast to impact delivery
findings.detail: The strategy acknowledges that expenditure within capital schemes may slip because 'Multiple schemes within the capital programme are still in development stages' and warns that 'due to significant cost increases in many capital programmes at tender stages there is likely to be a significant impact on the delivery of schemes within the Capital Programme.'
findings.matters: Cost inflation and delivery slippage can change borrowing forecasts and reserve drawdown timing. Unfunded cost overruns or stalled schemes create revenue pressure or force re-borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Current forecasts: £11.460m earmarked reserves and £11.118m capital receipts (2025-26); £16.639m earmarked reserves and £7.887m capital receipts (2026-27)
findings.quote: Multiple schemes within the capital programme are still in development stages and therefore expenditure may slip. Furthermore, due to significant cost increases in many capital programmes at tender stages there is likely to be a significant impact on the delivery of schemes within the Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Usable reserves projected to fall from £84.37m to £37.90m over three years (2026-2029).
findings.detail: Balance sheet resources in Table 2 show a steep decline as the council deploys reserves to fund capital expenditure. This leaves the council increasingly dependent on external borrowing as the forecast period advances.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce a council's financial flexibility and buffer against unexpected costs, making it more vulnerable to service shocks and more reliant on access to credit markets.
findings.figures: Balance Sheet Resources: 31 March 2026 £84.37m, 31 March 2027 £58.79m, 31 March 2028 £41.62m, 31 March 2029 £37.90m
findings.quote: Less: Balance Sheet Resources (84.37) (58.79) (41.62) (37.90)

findings.headline: Borrowing requirement jumps to £50.72m in 2026-27 and continues rising through the forecast period.
findings.detail: The council's net borrowing need was zero in 2025-26, but Table 2 forecasts £50.72m required in 2026-27, £75.52m in 2027-28, and £78.83m in 2028-29. This is driven by capital expenditure outpacing reserves and other funding sources.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's debt trajectory and what is driving it. A shift from net investment to significant new borrowing signals tightening reserves and capital-led spending pressure.
findings.quote: The council is currently forecasting a new borrowing requirement in 2026-27 of £50.72 million with a further requirement in the next two years

findings.headline: Council faces demographic pressures including ageing population and young people with complex disabilities; inflation significantly impacts tender costs
findings.detail: The strategic context identifies 'demographic pressures including an ageing population, an increasing number of young people with complex disabilities living into adulthood and requiring care and support' alongside 'the ongoing cost of living crisis.' The document states: 'Inflation has had a significant impact particularly in relation to capital costs and tender pricing.' These factors are expected to persist, placing ongoing pressure on both revenue and capital budgets.
findings.matters: Structural demographic shifts driving service demand growth combined with elevated inflation and tender costs create persistent revenue budget pressure and uncertainty over future service affordability, beyond the current planning period.
findings.figures: Council population approximately 146,000. Ageing population trend and increasing complex disability cohort cited as ongoing pressures.
findings.quote: The Council continues to face significant challenges. These include demographic pressures including an ageing population, an increasing number of young people with complex disabilities living into adulthood and requiring care and support, the need for the public sector to decarbonise by 2030 as well as the ongoing cost of living crisis. Inflation has had a significant impact particularly in relation to capital costs and tender pricing.

findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio identified as management-intensive and geographically concentrated, generating poor returns
findings.detail: Investment properties valued at £4.890m generate only £458,500 annual income (approximately 9.4% gross yield, but described as management-intensive with high unit count relative to income). The strategy notes: 'The portfolio therefore does not accord with the risk balance in location and sectoral terms to the majority of investment portfolios and is also management intensive, with a large number of units relative to the overall income and value.' All assets are within the County Borough (zero diversification).
findings.matters: Poor-yielding, concentrated, management-intensive investments represent inefficient deployment of assets and capital; they constrain resources available for core service or asset rationalisation while generating minimal revenue benefit.
findings.figures: Investment Properties value: £4.890m. Forecast rental income: £458,500 pa. Ratio to net revenue budget 2026-27: 0.11% (down from 0.12% in 2025-26).
findings.quote: The portfolio therefore does not accord with the risk balance in location and sectoral terms to the majority of investment portfolios and is also management intensive, with a large number of units relative to the overall income and value.

findings.headline: New capital projects scope limited without full external funding, grants or external contributions
findings.detail: The affordability section states: 'there is limited scope for new capital projects unless fully funded from grants and external contributions.' The strategy notes 'uncertain' revenue budget settlements beyond the current year and states: 'Given the uncertainty over future capital receipts, diminishing uncommitted earmarked reserves and limited capital budget allocations from Welsh Government, this will mean that there is limited scope for new capital projects.'
findings.matters: An explicit affordability constraint on future investment signals revenue budget stress and limited capacity to absorb service demands or additional capital pressures without reducing services or raising borrowing further.
findings.figures: The strategy references ongoing cost of living crisis, challenging financial settlements, and diminishing reserves as drivers of this constraint.
findings.quote: there is limited scope for new capital projects unless fully funded from grants and external contributions. This must be a factor considered by Council when determining the Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Limited capital receipts declining from £21.38m (2025-26) to £4.77m (2029-30), constraining funding flexibility
findings.detail: Table 6 shows capital receipts forecast to decline sharply over the period. Opening balance 2025-26 is £21.38m, with applied receipts of £10.18m in 2026-27 leaving only £11.20m. By 2029-30 this falls to £4.77m. The strategy explicitly states the Council 'has limited capital assets which it could sell' and notes 'the majority of capital receipts from asset sales are already allocated to the capital programme.'
findings.matters: Declining capital receipts reduce the Council's ability to fund schemes without borrowing, increasing reliance on external debt and reducing financial flexibility during the forecast period.
findings.quote: The Council does have a Disposal Strategy, though has limited capital assets which it could sell and use receipts to reinvest.

findings.headline: £121.82m capital programme in 2026-27 requires £16.20m new borrowing for school projects, with cost inflation risk materialising
findings.detail: The capital programme is heavily weighted to a £106.62m Sustainable Communities for Learning scheme across four schools (2026-27 to 2027-28). The strategy states the Council will borrow approximately £16.20m for new school projects. Separately, the risk section identifies that 'costs potentially exceeding available budgets' from construction inflation, supply chain difficulties, and wage pressures. The document warns that schemes 'may need to be reprioritised based on the available funding' if procurement reveals higher costs.
findings.matters: Large committed schemes with multi-year delivery risk combined with real cost inflation creates material exposure to budget slippage or scheme deferral, affecting both capital programme completion and revenue servicing assumptions.
findings.figures: £121.82m total 2026-27 expenditure; £106.62m for Sustainable Communities for Learning (four schools) 2026-27 to 2027-28; £16.20m new borrowing for schools; £19.37m Porthcawl Grand Pavilion 2026-27 to 2027-28.
findings.quote: The Council will need to borrow approximately £16.20 million in order to fund new school projects in line with the Council's Schools Modernisation Programme.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs rising as proportion of revenue budget, with explicit concern about future borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Table 10 shows capital financing costs (net) rising from 1.97% of revenue in 2025-26 to 2.06% by 2029-30. The strategy explicitly states: 'An increasing ratio limits the scope for additional borrowing in future years and reduces the Council's overall flexibility when making decisions on the allocation of its revenue resources.' The document further warns: 'it will be increasingly difficult to secure revenue funding to meet the costs of any new borrowing.'
findings.matters: Rising financing costs constrain future flexibility and signal mounting debt service pressure relative to available revenue, which is material for credit assessment and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Capital financing costs: 1.97% (2025-26) rising to 2.06% (2029-30). CFR forecast increase of £16.31m in 2026-27.
findings.quote: An increasing ratio limits the scope for additional borrowing in future years and reduces the Council's overall flexibility when making decisions on the allocation of its revenue resources.

findings.headline: Welsh Government capital funding increase is modest and insufficient for identified pressures
findings.detail: Welsh Government's capital allocation increased from £4.772 million to £4.992 million for 2026-27 (a £220,000 increase) and is described as modest. This increase is set against multiple cost pressures that could outpace funding growth.
findings.matters: Funding growth that lags inflation and identified cost pressures signals the Council will face tighter capital constraints and may need to borrow or defer schemes.
findings.figures: £4.772 million to £4.992 million; future estimates remain at increased level
findings.quote: Welsh Government's capital funding allocation to the Council for 2026-27 shows a slight increase to that previously anticipated, from £4.772 million to £4.992 million, and future estimates show funding as remaining at this increased level. It is a modest increase

findings.headline: Capital receipts are largely committed, constraining new scheme funding
findings.detail: The Council's capital receipts are heavily allocated to existing schemes within the capital programme. This limits the Council's ability to fund new capital schemes without additional borrowing. The Council notes that funding new schemes is challenging and may require securing specific grants and other external funding.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether a council has flexibility to fund capital investment or whether it must borrow for incremental needs, which adds to debt service costs.
findings.figures: Capital receipts largely committed to existing schemes; Welsh Government funding at £4.992 million for 2026-27
findings.quote: with the Council's capital receipts largely committed to schemes within the capital programme, funding any new schemes is challenging

findings.headline: Dependency on SEWCJC accounts which have had recurring quality and timing delays
findings.detail: The council consolidates transactions and balances from the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee. The auditor noted 'delays in certification...due to the late submission...and longer than anticipated audit periods due to the quality of those draft accounts'. For 2025-26, 'SEWCJC accounts production remains a risk for the preparation of the Council's financial statements particularly with the certification deadline coming forward to the end of September 2026'.
findings.matters: A council's consolidated accounts depend on timely, high-quality information from partner bodies. When partners have demonstrated quality issues, it creates risk that the council's own reporting will be delayed or contain errors.
findings.figures: SEWCJC is material enough to consolidate into the council's Statement of Accounts, affecting CIES, Balance Sheet and MIRS
findings.quote: The delay in certification has been due to the late submission of the SEWCJC draft accounts and longer than anticipated audit periods due to the quality of those draft accounts and complexity of transactions contained within them. Looking forward to next year, the timeliness of the SEWCJC accounts production remains a risk for the preparation of the Council's financial statements for 2025-26 particularly with the certification deadline coming forward to the end of September 2026.

findings.headline: Audit deadline moving to 30 September 2026; working paper timeliness is potential issue; council depends on SEWCJC for consolidated figures
findings.detail: The auditor explicitly warned that working paper preparation timeliness is a 'potential issue in achieving the deadlines for future years' when the audit window compresses further. The council currently struggles to have all working papers ready at audit start, and depends on the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee (SEWCJC) for consolidated figures, which itself has had quality and timeliness issues.
findings.matters: Audit deadline failures create uncertainty in financial reporting timelines and can flag governance or operational capacity issues; missing deadlines puts pressure on the council's ability to report accurately.
findings.figures: Deadline moving to 31 October 2025 for 2024-25; further acceleration to 30 September 2026 for 2025-26
findings.quote: We are conscious that when the accounts production and audit window reduce next year, this could be a potential issue in achieving the deadlines for future years.

findings.headline: Repeated errors in asset valuation spreadsheets despite three years of audit recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor noted errors in property revaluation spreadsheets for the third consecutive year. Although described as 'trivial' and totalling £252k understatement, the report states 'This year we again identified errors within the revaluation spreadsheets as a result of incorrect formulas'. The council has been implementing a new asset management system to address this, but the pattern of recurrence suggests control weaknesses in the current process.
findings.matters: Repeated control failures on asset valuations—even if individually immaterial—indicate systemic weaknesses in financial controls and suggest risk of undetected errors in other areas.
findings.figures: £252,000 total understatement from spreadsheet formula errors; £1.517 million and £2.369 million corrections to asset valuations
findings.quote: In 2022-23 and 2023-24, we reported issues arising from our audit of property, plant and equipment... This year we again we identified errors within the revaluation spreadsheets as a result of incorrect formulas used (as opposed to errors in the revaluations themselves as set out in Appendix 2). These were trivial and amounted to understatements of £252k in total.

findings.headline: Borrowing figures required significant audit corrections and working papers had clarity issues
findings.detail: The auditor identified that working papers for borrowings were 'not clear and concise and required revision after submission' and there were 'significant delays in responding to audit queries in these areas'. A £2.389m understatement of non-current borrowing was corrected by management. Given that borrowing is material to a council's financial position, the combination of working paper quality issues and large corrections suggests controls around borrowing accounting need attention.
findings.matters: A lender depends on accurate, clearly-documented borrowing figures. Weak working papers and significant post-audit corrections indicate control or documentation weaknesses that could mask other issues.
findings.figures: £2.389 million understatement of non-current borrowing corrected; £8.712 million carrying amount and £8.764 million fair value of short-term financial liabilities incorrectly excluded from disclosure
findings.quote: Two areas of particular concern were borrowings and cash where the working papers were not clear and concise and required revision after submission to us. There were also significant delays in responding to audit queries in these areas, which extended the time required for the audit.

news_drafts.headline: Bridgend plans £8.5m borrowing for 2026-27 capital programme and covers £99.5m of need from its own cash
news_drafts.lead:
Bridgend County Borough Council's Cabinet is being given a revised capital programme (money spent on things that last, such as buildings, roads and vehicles) of £86.752m for 2026-27. Of that, £8.489m is to be paid for by borrowing, about 9.8% of the programme. The Cabinet meets on 20 October 2026.

The borrowing splits into £4.640m of unsupported borrowing, which the government does not support, and £3.849m of supported borrowing. The capital report for the second quarter of 2026-27 lists both as the council's own resources for the programme.

A separate appendix covers the council's capital financing requirement (the total it has spent on long-lived assets that it has not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow). It puts the estimate for 2026-27 at £207.026m, against estimated gross debt of £107.516m. The £99.510m gap is met from the council's own cash. The appendix says: "The capital borrowing need (Capital Financing Requirement) has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This is known as Internal Borrowing."

news_drafts.headline: Bridgend's 2025-26 accounts receive unqualified audit opinion
news_drafts.lead: The Auditor General for Wales intends to issue an unqualified audit opinion on Bridgend's 2025-26 accounts, confirming they give a true and fair view and were properly prepared. However, auditors identified several control weaknesses. The initial draft accounts did not include transactions and balances from the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee, a shared body run with other councils, which were added only in a revised draft submitted in September. Auditors found that a category of asset valuations had not been properly indexed, a control gap that could become cumulatively significant over the five-year valuation cycle, though the current-year impact is not significant. Additionally, the minimum revenue provision—the amount set aside annually from the budget to repay borrowing—was understated by £0.291 million due to the accounting treatment of the Rhiw property purchase. All issues were corrected during the audit.

news_drafts.headline: Bridgend's 2025-26 accounts certified early, but audit found multiple errors in draft figures
news_drafts.lead: Bridgend Council's external auditors are certifying the 2025-26 accounts on 25 September, six days ahead of the statutory 30 September deadline. The Governance and Audit Committee was told that auditors had identified a series of misstatements in the draft accounts, all later corrected by council officers. These included member allowances overstated by £0.061 million, minimum revenue provision (the amount the council must set aside from each year's budget to repay past borrowing) understated by £0.291 million, transactions from the South East Wales Corporate Joint Committee initially omitted, and property valuations that had not been updated. The auditor also flagged that indexation, the annual revaluation uplift applied to council property assets, has not been applied to a category of existing use value assets and could become cumulatively material over five years. The council's previous year accounts received a clean bill of health from auditors.
